facts.statement: Bajadasaurus lived in northern Patagonia, Argentina, during the Early Cretaceous between 145 and 132.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Bajadasaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous epoch (late Berriasian to Valanginian stages, between 145 and 132.9 million years ago) of northern Patagonia, Argentina.

facts.statement: The only known specimen was excavated in 2010 by paleontologists from the Argentinian National Scientific and Technical Research Council (CONICET).
facts.quote: The only specimen of the dinosaur genus Bajadasaurus was excavated in 2010 by palaeontologists of the CONICET (National Scientific and Technical Research Council), the science agency of the Argentinian government.

facts.statement: The specimen was found at the Bajada Colorada locality, 40 km south of Picún Leufú near the Limay River in Patagonia.
facts.quote: The specimen was discovered in the Bajada Colorada locality, 40 km south of the town of Picún Leufú, near the western bank of the Limay River, in Patagonia.

facts.statement: Argentinian paleontologist Pablo Gallina discovered the specimen, which initially showed only some teeth.
facts.quote: The specimen, of which only some teeth were initially exposed, was found by Argentinian palaeontologist Pablo Gallina.

facts.statement: The specimen is curated by the Museo Municipal Ernesto Bachmann in Villa El Chocón, Neuquén Province, with the catalog number MMCh-PV 75.
facts.quote: The specimen is now curated by the Museo Municipal Ernesto Bachmann in Villa El Chocón, Neuquén Province, under the specimen number MMCh-PV 75.

facts.statement: The discovery attracted widespread international media attention due to the animal's spectacular spines.
facts.quote: Because of the spectacular spines, the discovery of Bajadasaurus was widely reported on by international news media.

facts.statement: Bajadasaurus possessed extremely elongated, two-pronged neural spines extending from its neck.
facts.quote: Bajadasaurus sported bifurcated (two-pronged), extremely elongated neural spines extending from the neck.

facts.statement: Its slender skull contained approximately 48 pencil-shaped teeth restricted to the front of the jaws.
facts.quote: The skull was slender and equipped with around 48 teeth that were pencil-shaped and restricted to the front of the jaws.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested in 2019 that the elongated spines of Bajadasaurus and Amargasaurus may have served as passive defense against predators.
facts.quote: The 2019 description of Bajadasaurus suggested they could have served as a passive defense against predators in both genera.

facts.statement: The eye openings were visible from the top, possibly allowing the animal to look forward while feeding.
facts.quote: The eye openings of Bajadasaurus were exposed in top view, possibly allowing the animal to look forwards while feeding.

facts.statement: As a dicraeosaurid, Bajadasaurus was a large, four-legged herbivore with a long neck, tail, and relatively tiny head.
facts.quote: As with all sauropods, dicraeosaurids were large, four-legged herbivores with a long neck and tail and a relatively tiny head.

facts.statement: Bajadasaurus was small compared to most sauropods, reaching roughly the size of an Asian elephant, and had a comparatively short neck.
facts.quote: They were small compared to most other sauropods, reaching roughly the size of present-day Asian elephants, and their neck was comparatively short.

facts.statement: As of 2019, the Bajadasaurus skull was the most complete dicraeosaurid skull known.
facts.quote: As of 2019, it is the most complete skull of a dicraeosaurid known.

facts.statement: The prefrontal bone contributed less to the eye socket and was smaller and less robust than in Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus.
facts.quote: The contribution of the prefrontal to the orbit was smaller than in Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus; the bone was also smaller and less robust than in these genera.

facts.statement: The elongated downward process of the squamosal bone distinguishes Bajadasaurus from other dicraeosaurids.
facts.quote: The downward projecting process of the squamosal, a bone forming the upper rear corner of the skull, was elongated, distinguishing the genus from other dicraeosaurids.

facts.statement: The basisphenoid possessed slender basipterygoid processes that extended forward and downward to brace the braincase against the palate.
facts.quote: The basisphenoid, which formed part of the underside of the braincase, had a pair of gracile bony extensions, the basipterygoid processes, which extended forwards and downwards to articulate with the pterygoid of the palate, bracing the braincase against the latter.

facts.statement: The basipterygoid processes were a unique feature of the genus, being more than six times longer than they were wide.
facts.quote: An autapomorphy of the genus, these processes were longer and more slender than in Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus, being more than six times long than wide.

facts.statement: While several functions have been proposed for the spines in related Amargasaurus, the 2019 description suggests they served as passive defense in both Bajadasaurus and Amargasaurus.
facts.quote: Several possible functions have been proposed for these spines in Amargasaurus; the 2019 description of Bajadasaurus suggested they could have served as a passive defense against predators in both genera.

facts.statement: Bajadasaurus had a lower jaw that was approximately 80% the length of its skull.
facts.quote: The lower jaw was ca. 80% the length of the skull

facts.statement: The teeth of Bajadasaurus pronuspinax had an average replacement time of about 40.7 days.
facts.quote: The teeth of Bajadasaurus pronuspinax had a mean replacement time of about 40.7 days.

facts.statement: A single preserved neck vertebra of Bajadasaurus has an extremely elongated neural spine that is 58 cm long, making the vertebra four times taller than it is long.
facts.quote: This neural spine is 58 cm long and made the vertebra four times taller than it was long.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the elongated neck spines of Bajadasaurus were likely covered by a horny sheath, similar to those of Amargasaurus.
facts.quote: Although similar striations cannot be observed on the spines of Bajadasaurus due to poor preservation, Gallina and colleagues found it likely that the spines were covered by a horny sheath as well.

facts.statement: Bajadasaurus belongs to the family Dicraeosauridae, which is one of the three principal families within the sauropod subdivision Diplodocoidea.
facts.quote: Dicraeosaurids are one of the three principal families comprising the Diplodocoidea, a major subdivision of sauropod dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Bajadasaurus is distinguished from other dicraeosaurids by four unique anatomical features known as autapomorphies.
facts.quote: Bajadasaurus itself can be differentiated from other dicraeosaurids by a unique combination of features, which includes four autapomorphies

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Whitlock and Mantilla placed Bajadasaurus as the most basal member of a specific clade within Dicraeosauridae, differing from earlier classifications.
facts.quote: A subsequent analysis by John Whitlock and Jeffrey Wilson Mantilla, in 2020, found Bajadasaurus to be the most basal member of a clade that also contains Lingwulong and the unnamed North American taxon MOR 592.

facts.statement: A 2022 study by Windholz found conflicting phylogenetic results, with one analysis suggesting Bajadasaurus is closely related to other South American dicraeosaurids like Amargatitanis and Pilmatueia.
facts.quote: A 2022 study led by Guillermo Windholz analyzed multiple datasets and found conflicting results, with one of their analyses finding Bajadasaurus to be most closely related to Amargatitanis and Pilmatueia in a clade of South American dicraeosaurids.

facts.statement: The analysis determined that Bajadasaurus is the sister taxon to a clade consisting of Pilmatueia and an unresolved derived group including Amargasaurus, Brachytrachelopan, and Dicraeosaurus.
